ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was approved by the Makerere University School of Biomedical Sciences Research and Ethics Committee (SBS-REC) at its meeting of 16 November 2023 (reference SBS-2023-452; approval valid from 12 February 2024 to 12 February 2025).
MO, who chairs the SBS-REC, did not take part in the committee's review of this protocol.
All data were collected after this clearance and within the period of ethics approval.
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants were enrolled between May and June 2024, after administrative clearance had been granted by the hospital.
Pregnant women admitted for delivery at KNRH on data collection days were eligible if they gave written informed consent, irrespective of their hepatitis B vaccination history.
All participants were aged 18 years or older.
Participants were selected by systematic random sampling.
All participants provided written informed consent before enrolment.
A total of 418 women were enrolled, against a target of 420; refusals were not recorded in the study database.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: For the prevalence of protective anti-HBs levels, Kish's formula [22], n = Z²p(1 -p)/d², with an assumed non-protective prevalence of 22.9% as used in a previous Ugandan study [20], Z = 1.96 and a precision (d) of 5%, gave a minimum of 272 participants. For the analysis of associated factors, a sample size for comparing two proportions computed in G*Power (two-sided α 0.05, 80% power, expected proportions 0.192 and 0.052) gave 383 participants. The larger requirement was adopted, and the enrolment target was set at 420 to allow for incomplete questionnaires or unusable samples.

text.text: Mother-to-child transmission sustains the burden of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in sub-Saharan Africa, yet little is known about whether women giving birth in Uganda are protected.

We estimated the prevalence of protective hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) levels, described serological profiles and identified associated factors among women admitted for delivery at Kawempe National Referral Hospital, Kampala.
In this cross-sectional study, 418 women were selected by systematic random sampling in 2024 and interviewed about sociodemographic characteristics, hepatitis B testing, vaccination and exposures.
Anti-HBs was quantified by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (protective: ≥10 mIU/mL); other HBV markers were screened with a rapid test.
Prevalence ratios were estimated with modified Poisson regression.
Overall, 264 women (63.2%) reported vaccination: 203 during the current pregnancy and 61 before it only.

Protective levels were found in 322 women (77.0%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 72.8-80.8): 50.6% of never-vaccinated women, 82.0% of those vaccinated before the current pregnancy only and 95.6% of those vaccinated during it.

After adjustment, vaccination before the current pregnancy only (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.54; 95% CI 1.24-1.89) and during it (1.86; 95% CI 1.57-2.20) were associated with protection; no sociodemographic or behavioural factor was.
Eighty-two women (19.6%) had no serological evidence of immunity or infection; 65 had never been vaccinated.

Of 300 women who reported a previous negative test, 50 (16.7%) had never been vaccinated, and 68 of 250 vaccinated women with known completion status (27.2%) had not completed three doses, mostly because they were not told to return or forgot.
The rapid test detected hepatitis B surface antigen in 21 women (5.0%), but discordant marker patterns suggest some false positives.
One in five women reached delivery susceptible to HBV, largely because a negative test was not followed by vaccination.
Linking every negative antenatal test to vaccination could close much of this gap.
Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a leading cause of cirrhosis and liver cancer worldwide.
In 2022, an estimated 254 million people were living with chronic HBV infection and 1.1 million died of HBV-related causes [1].

text.text: Knowing how many women reach delivery unprotected, and where the screening-to-vaccination pathway fails, is needed to target antenatal interventions.

This study aimed to determine the prevalence of protective anti-HBs levels and of serological profiles of immunity, infection and susceptibility, and the factors associated with protective anti-HBs levels, among women admitted for delivery at Kawempe National Referral Hospital (KNRH).
We conducted a hospital-based cross-sectional study.
Participants were enrolled between May and June 2024, after administrative clearance had been granted by the hospital.
The study is reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline [21] (S1 Checklist).
text.formatted: The study is reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[21]</ref> (S1 Checklist).

text.text: KNRH is a public, urban, specialised national referral and teaching hospital in Kampala, Uganda.
Its maternity services include antenatal care, delivery, postnatal care, routine immunisation and child growth monitoring.
About 2,100 women give birth at the hospital each month, of whom about 25% are referred from other facilities or self-referred.
Pregnant women admitted for delivery at KNRH on data collection days were eligible if they gave written informed consent, irrespective of their hepatitis B vaccination history.
Women receiving treatment for HBV infection and women in active labour were excluded.
All participants were aged 18 years or older.
Participants were selected by systematic random sampling.

The sampling interval was calculated by dividing the expected number of admissions for delivery during the data collection period (about 80 per day) by the required sample size, which gave an interval of 3.8, rounded to 4.
Every fourth woman admitted on a data collection day was approached; a woman who declined was replaced by the next woman admitted.
Participants' files were marked to prevent re-enrolment.

For the prevalence of protective anti-HBs levels, Kish's formula [22], n = Z²p(1 -p)/d², with an assumed non-protective prevalence of 22.9% as used in a previous Ugandan study [20], Z = 1.96 and a precision (d) of 5%, gave a minimum of 272 participants.

text.text: For the analysis of associated factors, a sample size for comparing two proportions computed in G*Power (two-sided α 0.05, 80% power, expected proportions 0.192 and 0.052) gave 383 participants.
The larger requirement was adopted, and the enrolment target was set at 420 to allow for incomplete questionnaires or unusable samples.
The primary outcome was a protective anti-HBs level, defined as an anti-HBs concentration of at least 10 mIU/mL (10 IU/L) [5].
text.formatted: The primary outcome was a protective anti-HBs level, defined as an anti-HBs concentration of at least 10 mIU/mL (10 IU/L) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Women who were HBsAg-negative were further classified by their combination of anti-HBs and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) results: vaccine-type immunity (anti-HBc-negative, anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL), immunity after past infection (anti-HBcpositive, anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL), past infection without protective anti-HBs (anti-HBc-positive, anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL) and susceptible (anti-HBc-negative, anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL).

text.text: Secondary outcomes were the prevalence of HBsAg, HBeAg, hepatitis B e antibody (anti-HBe) and anti-HBc.

The following variables from the questionnaire (S1 File) were analysed: age (recorded in the categories 18-30, 31-40, 41-50 and 51 years or older), education, marital status, residence, previous caesarean delivery, attendance at all scheduled antenatal visits, alcohol use, smoking, self-reported chronic medical condition (including HIV, cancer, sickle cell disease or other chronic disease), previous blood transfusion, previous surgery, having cared for a person with hepatitis B, recreational drug use, multiple sexual partners, sharing of sharp objects, previous hepatitis B testing and its result, and self-reported past hepatitis B. Follow-up items asked only of subgroups (number of antenatal visits among women who had missed visits, reasons for not being vaccinated during the current pregnancy, injection drug use, safer sex practice and initiation of hepatitis B treatment) and two items on perceived availability and quality of antenatal hepatitis B services were not analysed for this paper.
Hepatitis B vaccination status was derived from two questions and classified as never vaccinated, vaccinated before the current pregnancy only, or vaccinated during the current pregnancy.
Among vaccinated women, completion of three doses, the schedule used and reasons for non-completion were recorded.
Vaccination history was self-reported and checked against hospital records where these were available.
A structured questionnaire was pretested among 10 pregnant women at Kajjansi Health Centre IV, Wakiso District, and revised before use.

It was administered in face-to-face interviews by the principal investigator and two research assistants (a laboratory technologist and a nurse), who were trained on the tool, quality control and sample handling.
The principal investigator reviewed all questionnaires daily for completeness and consistency.
From each participant, 4 mL of venous blood was drawn into an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tube and centrifuged at 3,000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the plasma was separated into cryovials.
Plasma was screened on site with a rapid lateral-flow (immunochromatographic) fivemarker hepatitis B test cassette (Dewei Medical Equipment Co.
Ltd, China) that qualitatively detects HBsAg, anti-HBs, HBeAg, anti-HBe and anti-HBc.
Tests were read visually according to the manufacturer's instructions and were valid only if the control line appeared.

The manufacturer reports a sensitivity of 98.7% and a specificity of 99.1% for HBsAg; performance data for the other markers were not available, and no confirmatory enzyme immunoassay, HBV DNA or alanine aminotransferase testing was performed.

The remaining plasma was stored at -80 °C at the Department of Pharmacology and Therapeutics, Makerere University, and transported in cold boxes to the Nakasero Blood Bank laboratory, where anti-HBs was quantified with the Elecsys Anti-HBs assay on an Elecsys 2010 analyser (Roche Diagnostics GmbH, Mannheim, Germany).
This is a double-antigen sandwich electrochemiluminescence immunoassay with a measuring range of 2-1,000 IU/L; results of 10 IU/L (equivalent to 10 mIU/mL) or more were classified as protective.
The analyser was calibrated and quality control samples were run before each batch, and 50 µL of plasma per sample was analysed according to the manufacturer's instructions.
NumPy version 2.5 and SciPy version 1.18.
Categorical variables were summarised as frequencies and percentages with numerators and denominators, and prevalences were reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CI).
Anti-HBs concentrations were truncated at the limits of the assay measuring range and were not normally distributed, so they were summarised as median and interquartile range (IQR).

Characteristics were compared between women with and without protective anti-HBs levels, and between HBsAg-positive and HBsAg-negative women, with Pearson's chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test when any expected cell count was below 5 (Monte Carlo estimate with 100,000 samples for tables larger than 2 × 2).

Because the outcome was common, associations with protective anti-HBs levels were estimated as prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% CI using modified Poisson regression, that is, a generalised linear model with a Poisson distribution, log link and robust (sandwich) variance estimator [23].

The study protocol was approved by the Makerere University School of Biomedical Sciences Research and Ethics Committee (SBS-REC) at its meeting of 16 November 2023 (reference SBS-2023-452; approval valid from 12 February 2024 to 12 February 2025).
MO, who chairs the SBS-REC, did not take part in the committee's review of this protocol.
Administrative clearance to conduct the study at KNRH was granted by the Executive Director of the hospital on 17 May 2024 (reference ED.01/04/024).
All data were collected after this clearance and within the period of ethics approval.
All participants provided written informed consent before enrolment.
Under the approved protocol, women found to be infected were to be referred to a physician for further management; vaccination was not provided as part of the study.
Personal identifiers were replaced with unique study codes, and the data were stored on password-protected computers accessible only to the study team.
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
A total of 418 women were enrolled, against a target of 420; refusals were not recorded in the study database.
Most were aged 18-40 years (338/418, 80.9%), 187 (44.7%) had tertiary education and 250 (59.8%) lived in urban areas (Table 1).

In addition, only 2 of the 49 women who reported a previous positive test were HBsAg-positive in this study, whereas 14 of the 21 HBsAg-positive women had reported a previous negative test.

Among the 397 HBsAg-negative women, 287 (72.3%) had vaccine-type immunity, 20 (5.0%) had immunity after past infection, 8 (2.0%) had anti-HBc without protective anti-HBs, and 82 (20.7%; 95% CI 17.0-24.9) were susceptible (Table 2).

text.text: 289 Discussion 290 In this study of women admitted for delivery at a national referral hospital in Uganda, 77.0% had 291 protective anti-HBs levels, but one in five (19.6%) had no serological evidence of either 292 immunity or infection and was therefore susceptible to HBV.
Four in five of these susceptible 293 women had never been vaccinated.
Vaccination was strongly associated with protection, and almost all women vaccinated during the current pregnancy were protected.
No sociodemographic or behavioural characteristic was independently associated with protection.
Our data show where the pathway from testing to protection breaks down.
The largest gap was failure to vaccinate.

One in six women who reported a negative hepatitis B test had never been vaccinated, and 57 unvaccinated women had never been tested at all, despite the availability of free adult screening and vaccination since 2015 [14].
text.formatted: One in six women who reported a negative hepatitis B test had never been vaccinated, and 57 unvaccinated women had never been tested at all, despite the availability of free adult screening and vaccination since 2015 <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Women who had been tested were far more likely to be protected than those who had not (86.0% vs 31.9%; Table 1), consistent with testing being the usual route to vaccination.
text.formatted: Women who had been tested were far more likely to be protected than those who had not (86.0% vs 31.9%; Table <ref type="table">1</ref>), consistent with testing being the usual route to vaccination.

text.text: Associations of protection with previous surgery, caesarean delivery, blood transfusion and full antenatal attendance in bivariable analysis disappeared after adjustment for vaccination.
This suggests that contact with health services matters mainly because it creates opportunities for testing and vaccination.
Offering the first vaccine dose at the antenatal visit at which a negative result is returned would address this gap directly.
The second gap was an incomplete vaccine series.

A quarter of vaccinated women had not completed three doses, and the reasons they gave were mostly health-system failures rather than refusal: they were not told to return, they forgot, or the vaccine was out of stock.
Similar barriers, together with vaccine hesitancy, have been described among pregnant women in Kampala, in other Ugandan populations [16, 24] and across sub-Saharan Africa [15].

text.text: Most women followed the 0, 1 and 6 month schedule, which cannot be completed before delivery if it is started after the first trimester.
Schedules with shorter intervals between doses are acceptable for adults [5, 17].
text.formatted: Schedules with shorter intervals between doses are acceptable for adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">17]</ref>.

text.text: Protection was more frequent among women vaccinated during the current pregnancy than among those vaccinated only before it.
This is consistent with a recent dose producing higher antibody concentrations, which then decline over time [19, 25].

text.text: A concentration below 10 mIU/mL in a previously vaccinated woman does not necessarily mean loss of protection, because people who responded to vaccination usually retain immune memory [5, 19].

text.text: The 17 vaccinated women classified as susceptible may therefore overstate true susceptibility.
Completion of three doses was not significantly associated with protection, possibly because of inaccurate recall of the number of doses.
Hepatitis B vaccination during pregnancy is safe [26].
text.formatted: Hepatitis B vaccination during pregnancy is safe <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[26]</ref>.

text.text: The proportion of women with protective levels (77.0%) exceeded the proportion who reported vaccination (63.2%) because half of the never-vaccinated women had protective levels.
Almost all of these women had a vaccine-type profile (anti-HBc-negative), so natural infection explains little of this immunity, although rapid anti-HBc testing may miss some past infections.

The most likely explanations are vaccination that women did not report or remember, including infant vaccination in the youngest women through the pentavalent vaccine [10], and misclassification of vaccination status.

text.text: This finding indicates that self-reported vaccination history is an unreliable guide to protection in this population.
The rapid test detected HBsAg in 5.0% of women, which is close to the pooled estimate of 4.9% for pregnant women in East Africa [7].
text.formatted: The rapid test detected HBsAg in 5.0% of women, which is close to the pooled estimate of 4.9% for pregnant women in East Africa <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[7]</ref>.

text.text: It is higher than the 3.0% reported among women nationally [9] and the prevalence found among pregnant women in south-western Uganda [11, 12], but lower than the 11.8% reported in northern Uganda [10].

text.text: However, this estimate must be interpreted with caution.
Most HBsAg-positive women also had protective anti-HBs, which is uncommon in true chronic infection.
Most HBeAg-positive women were HBsAg-negative, and anti-HBe was often found without anti-HBc; both patterns are biologically implausible.
Rapid HBsAg results also agreed poorly with women's reports of previous tests.
Together, these findings suggest that the rapid multi-marker test produced false-positive results, particularly for HBeAg and anti-HBe.
Because no confirmatory immunoassay or HBV DNA testing was performed, we cannot estimate the true prevalence of infection or the risk of transmission.
These results support WHO's recommendation that reactive rapid tests be confirmed before women are classified as infected and assessed for antiviral prophylaxis [6].
text.formatted: These results support WHO's recommendation that reactive rapid tests be confirmed before women are classified as infected and assessed for antiviral prophylaxis <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[6]</ref>.

text.text: The association between sharing sharp objects and HBsAg positivity is consistent with blood-borne transmission but is based on few cases.
This study did not evaluate interventions, so the following implications are based on the gaps we observed.
The main avoidable gap was that a negative test was not consistently followed by vaccination.
Linking every negative antenatal test to a first vaccine dose at the same visit, with reminders and a reliable vaccine supply, would directly address it.

Now that the hepatitis B birth dose is part of Uganda's routine schedule [13], newborns can be protected regardless of their mothers' immunity; antenatal testing therefore remains essential mainly to identify infected mothers, using confirmed results, so that eligible mothers receive antiviral prophylaxis [6].

text.text: Strengths of this study include systematic random sampling, quantitative measurement of anti-HBs with an automated immunoassay, cross-classification of anti-HBs with anti-HBc to distinguish vaccine-type from natural immunity, and reporting of all exposure and risk-factor variables collected.
The study also has limitations.

First, its cross-sectional design does not allow causal inference, and it was conducted at a single national referral hospital, so the findings may not be generalisable to women delivering at lower-level facilities.
Second, vaccination history and exposures were self-reported.
Vaccination cards were not systematically available, and the high prevalence of protection among never-vaccinated women indicates substantial misclassification.

Third, HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBe and anti-HBc were detected with a rapid test whose performance for markers other than HBsAg has not been validated, without confirmatory immunoassay, HBV DNA or alanine aminotransferase testing, and the discordant patterns we observed indicate false-positive results.

Fourth, HIV status was recorded only within a composite question on chronic illness, and body mass index, parity, diabetes and time since the last vaccine dose were not available, so residual confounding is possible.
Fifth, age was recorded in broad categories, and 11 women reported being 51 years or older, which may reflect misreporting.
Sixth, a single anti-HBs measurement cannot distinguish susceptible women from vaccinated women with waning antibody but intact immune memory.
Seventh, we did not record whether HBsAg-positive women were linked to care or whether their infants received prophylaxis, or whether susceptible women were later vaccinated.
Finally, refusals were not recorded, so participants could not be compared with women who declined.

Most women delivering at KNRH had protective anti-HBs levels, but one in five reached delivery with no serological evidence of immunity or infection, and most of these women had never been vaccinated.
The main avoidable gaps were that a negative test was not consistently followed by vaccination and that started vaccine series were not completed, largely for healthsystem reasons.

Linking every negative antenatal hepatitis B test to vaccination, and confirming reactive rapid tests before women are classified as infected, could strengthen efforts to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HBV in Uganda.
